extracted.intended_audience: IPR practitioners/patent attorneys (petitioners and patent owners) and PTAB decisionmakers
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment of whether the Board should decline discretionary denial of an IPR petition based on prosecution history, material error, prior-art consideration, claim construction, and unexpected-results arguments. Focused on showing when examiner error or applicant misconduct warrants institution despite prior prosecution interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advanced Bionics framework — first prong (same or substantially same art/arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the same or substantially the same art or arguments were presented to the Office during prosecution (the first prong of the Advanced Bionics test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the petition relies on combinations involving references that were not before the Examiner (or arguments not previously presented), the first prong is not satisfied and discretionary denial is inappropriate. Cited examples: Advanced Bionics, IPR2019-01469, Paper 6 at 8-9; Thorne Research, IPR2021-00491, Paper 18 at 8-9; Halliburton Energy Servs. v. U.S. Well Servs., IPR2021-01036, Paper 12 at 20; K/S HIMPP v. Bragi GmbH, IPR2023-01205, Paper 8 at 20; ResMed Inc. v. New York University, IPR2022-00990, Paper 16 at 15-16.

rubrics_metrics.name: Becton, Dickinson factors (material error analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Becton, Dickinson factors (a–f) to determine whether the Office committed material error during prosecution that weighs against discretionary denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether references were considered during prosecution (factor (c)), whether the record is silent (factor (e)), and other factors (including materiality under (f)). The Petition argues factors (c), (e), and (f) weigh in favor of finding material error here. See Advanced Bionics, IPR2019-01469, Paper 6 at 8; Klein Tools, IPR2024-01400 (silence in the record can show material error).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material error by applicant mischaracterizing prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner’s mischaracterizations or misleading statements during prosecution that cause the Examiner to err constitute material error and can defeat discretionary denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant misleads the Office into committing error (e.g., asserting a prior art reference is limited to second-line therapy when its published claims are not so limited), the Board has refused to exercise discretion to deny petitions. Examples: Samsung Bioepis Co. Ltd. v. Alexion Pharma. Inc., IPR2023-01070, Paper 9 at 66; Danisco US Inc. v. Novozymes A/S, IPR2019-01010; Dr. Falk Pharma v. Ellodi Pharmaceuticals, IPR2025-00056; Medtronic Corevalve LLC v. Speyside Medical, IPR2021-00239.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether a reference was meaningfully considered during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination if a prior-art reference was actually evaluated by the Examiner (not merely listed in an IDS); mere listing in an IDS is insufficient to show meaningful consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB decisions recognize that an Examiner’s mere receipt of an IDS does not equate to meaningful evaluation; if the Examiner overlooked or failed to substantively consider a key reference, that can be material error supporting institution. Cited cases: Dr. Reddy’s Labs. S.A. v. Eye Therapies, IPR2024-00467; Posco Co. Ltd. v. Arcelormittal, IPR2024-01376; Klein Tools, IPR2024-01400; Motorola Mobility, IPR2025-00040.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine references — POSA would combine where references suggest doing so
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSA) would have been motivated to combine the teachings of the prior art (e.g., combining a liposomal irinotecan teaching with a first-line regimen) based on the references themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a reference reports results in a different clinical setting (second-line), passages suggesting further testing or replacement (e.g., 'it seems logical to test ... replacing irinotecan in FOLFIRINOX with MM-398') can supply motivation to combine. Cropping quotes or attorney re-interpretation cannot rebut a POSA-based reading of the references. Evidence from POSA declarations (e.g., Dr. Ratain) carries weight; attorney argument does not. See Icon Health & Fitness, Inc. v. Strava, Inc., 849 F.3d 1034, 1043 (Fed. Cir. 2017).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success across different treatment stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the POSA would have had a reasonable expectation of success in applying teachings from one clinical stage (e.g., second-line therapy) to another (e.g., first-line therapy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owner arguments that first-line and second-line therapies are inherently different (different tolerability, patient condition, malignancy) must be weighed against explicit suggestions in the art to study/replace components across stages. If prosecution hinged on lack of reasonable expectation because of alleged stage differences, but the art suggests such combination, that prosecution argument may have misled the Examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — do method-of-treatment claims require clinical efficacy?
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim term 'method of treating' should be construed to require clinical efficacy in a human patient, or whether such a requirement improperly imports limitations from the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should not be read to require efficacy absent express disavowal or lexicography; reading an efficacy threshold into a 'method of treating' claim can be legally erroneous and materially affect patentability. See Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303, 1323 (Fed. Cir. 2005). If patent owner convinced Examiner to require evidence of clinical efficacy, that may have lowered the bar to allowance improperly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results must be substantial and supported to rebut obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting unexpected results (efficacy or tolerability) to rebut prima facie obviousness, the improvement must be substantial and supported by appropriate evidence from the viewpoint of a POSA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-filing references may be considered, but claimed improvements must be more than marginal; routine medical practices (e.g., dose reduction correlating with lower toxicity) weigh against finding unexpected results. Case law: Regeneron v. Mylan and Genentech precedent cited for routine medical practices being obvious in dosing contexts. Wainberg (post-filing) here is argued not to show substantial unexpected improvements; other post-filing refs (Nichetti, Nevala-Plegamm) further undercut unexpected-result claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney argument is not evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal principle that statements by counsel cannot substitute for factual evidence when interpreting prior art or asserting POSA understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board should not adopt positions based solely on attorney argument without supporting evidence; citations: Icon Health & Fitness, Inc. v. Strava, Inc., 849 F.3d 1034, 1043 (Fed. Cir. 2017).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner silence or lack of discussion in the record can show material error
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of discussion or analysis of key prior art in the prosecution record (silence) may indicate the Examiner overlooked or was misled about the art — supporting a finding of material error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB has found that 'silence' in the record about a reference can show material error (e.g., Klein Tools, IPR2024-01400). Where critical teachings were not traversed or considered in office actions or remarks, that omission supports declining discretionary denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material error includes misapprehending or overlooking specific teachings
rubrics_metrics.description: Material error encompasses the Examiner misapprehending or overlooking specific teachings of the relevant prior art during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advanced Bionics and subsequent PTAB decisions treat such misapprehension/overlooking as material error warranting institution. See Advanced Bionics, IPR2019-01469, Paper 6 at 8; Samsung, IPR2023-01070, Paper 9 at 66.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine optimization/standard practices in medicine weigh against non-obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-known, standard medical practices (e.g., dose variation, toxicity management) are routine and thus weigh against claims of non-obviousness based on expected improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that varying doses or standard responses to patient reactions are well-known and often obvious; such practices undermine unexpected-result or non-obviousness assertions. Cited authority: Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc., and Genentech v. Sandoz (dosing claims obvious where varying dose is routine).
